solutions.check: 28 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Dylan-like ice and pot exploitation

indicators.note: to exploit something is to work it for your own ends, so the letters are worked over into a new order

explanation.surface: A sneer at a drug-addled celebrity: ice and pot, both street drugs, being abused.
explanation.walkthrough: Ice (crystal meth) and pot (cannabis) look like drug slang, but they are just letters; 'and' simply joins them. Dylan here is the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas.
explanation.definitionFit: Dylan Thomas was a celebrated Welsh poet, so writing in his manner is being lyrical in verse.

clue.text: Film producer's outrageous crib – cool!

indicators.note: something outrageous is wildly out of order, so the letters are thrown out of their order

explanation.surface: A movie mogul shows off an extravagant home and everyone says 'cool!'
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay. Albert 'Cubby' Broccoli produced the James Bond films.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Broccoli was the American producer behind the long-running James Bond movie franchise, a specific example of the category.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Male engaged in a form of sex without regard to ethics

indicators.note: to be engaged in an activity is to be inside it, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A man indulging in a particular sex act with no thought for right or wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The male letter goes between 'a' and the sex act, giving A-M-ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Amoral describes someone lacking any moral sense at all, neither good nor bad but indifferent to principles of right conduct.

clue.text: A tabloid backing arsehole

indicators.note: going backwards, so the word is read from its end to its start, which in a down clue runs upwards

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper

explanation.surface: A newspaper supporting some contemptible person: Private Eye's view of tabloid politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' reads like a newspaper endorsing someone, but it turns the paper's name round. The Sun is Britain's best-selling tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: The crude word is the literal anatomical name for the opening at the end of the gut, here used in its body sense.

clue.text: Hot stuff associated with politician John

blocks.note: a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Something sizzling linked to a politician named John, the stuff of a tabloid scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Politician John' reads as one person, but John is the definition, American slang for a toilet; the politician is just a Tory.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang a john is a toilet, the same room or fixture otherwise called a loo or WC.

clue.text: Pitcher piss-artist overturned on Sun and Express reporters' heads

indicators.note: something overturned is upside down, so the word is read the wrong way round
a head is the top or front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: British slang for a drunkard; a sot is a habitual drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk staggering about over two tabloids' editors: Fleet Street boozing in miniature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piss-artist' is British slang for a drunk; it gives the letters, not the definition, though the answer is also a British insult. 'On' places one piece before the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who throws or pitches a ball or coin can be called a thrower, one who flings it upward.

clue.text: see 16ac.
Lament rashly consuming Cyclops' dairy produce

indicators.note: acting rashly is acting without order or care, so these letters come out jumbled
to consume is to take inside, so one piece swallows the other

blocks.note: Cyclops is the setter, who refers to themselves as me

explanation.surface: Someone grieving hastily while gobbling the setter's cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's pseudonym in a clue usually stands for ME or I; here ME goes inside the rearranged letters after EM.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmental is a Swiss cheese with large holes, and cheese is a product made from milk.

clue.text: Alley resident, star act off Broadway, finally accepted?

indicators.note: something off is gone bad or out of kilter, so the letters are put into a new order
finally points to the end, so only the last letter of the word is kept
to accept something is to take it in, so a letter is received inside the rest

explanation.surface: A performer's headline act, banished from New York's theatre district, finds acceptance at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off Broadway' looks like the theatre term, but 'off' rearranges the star act and Broadway only lends its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A homeless feline typically lives among back streets and bins, the classic alley cat of cartoons and songs.

clue.text: Rogue artist's diminished state

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is a crossword artist; the 's adds S
California cut down to its short form

explanation.surface: A disreputable painter has come down in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diminished state' reads as a sorry condition, but it is a US state shortened: CAL is the abbreviation for California.
explanation.definitionFit: A rogue and a rascal are both mischievous, dishonest people, near synonyms for a likeable scoundrel or villain.

clue.text: (& 3dn.) Ace detectives' examination? The ultimate check

blocks.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace
the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: Top police detectives sitting an exam: the hardest assessment there is.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the plain-clothes detective branch of British police forces. The answer spans this square and 3 down.
explanation.definitionFit: An acid test is a decisive trial of worth, from using acid to prove whether metal is genuine gold.

clue.text: 'Love time' involved with unsocial kissing

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so all these letters are mixed together

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, the shape of O
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A romantic interlude ruined by someone antisocial during a kiss.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Love time' look like a phrase, but it is two single letters thrown in with the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Osculation is the formal, Latin-derived word for the act of pressing lips together, from osculum, little mouth.

clue.text: Climax on model's heavenly body

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a model's beautiful figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' looks like praise of a model's figure, but it is an astronomical object. In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A comet is an icy object orbiting the Sun, one of the celestial objects astronomers call heavenly bodies.

clue.text: Entrant is groomed for passing

indicators.note: grooming tidies and rearranges, so the letters are reworked into new order

explanation.surface: A competitor is being coached to pass an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like passing a test, but it means fleeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Transient and passing both describe something brief and short-lived, lasting only a while before it goes.

clue.text: (& 8dn.) Westminster flags?  They're not up to much presently

definitions.text: They're not up to much presently

blocks.note: flags are banners, and Westminster is home to Parliament

blocks.clueFragment: They're not up to much presently
blocks.note: the codes of conduct for MPs, which the setter thinks are currently low

explanation.walkthrough: Westminster is the seat of the UK Parliament; the question mark warns that flags means a different sort of standard. The second half is Private Eye's satirical swipe at MPs' behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is both a flag and a level of conduct, so the phrase means Parliament's banners and its ethical rules for members.

clue.text: Overly suspicious Celine needs a hit to come up

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means reading from the bottom upwards, the reverse order

blocks.note: a rap is a sharp knock

explanation.surface: A singer who wants a chart hit to make a comeback, and is anxious about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' looks like a hit record, but it is a blow. The singer's surname, a and the blow are joined and then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A paranoid person harbours unreasonable distrust of others, imagining plots and threats where none exist.

clue.text: Nuzzled Cyclops has to go down quickly

blocks.note: the setter has, contracted to I've without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: The setter has been snuggled up to and must hurry off.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name stands for I or ME; 'Cyclops has' becomes I've, apostrophe dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Planes or share prices take a steep, sudden plunge downward, plummeting toward the ground or bottom.

clue.text: Outline plan for suspect movement

indicators.note: movement means shifting about, so these letters move into a fresh order

blocks.note: pro is Latin for in favour of

explanation.surface: Police drawing up a scheme to track where a suspect goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect movement' reads as surveillance, but 'movement' rearranges the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospectus is a document describing a proposed venture or enterprise, setting out its scheme for investors or students.

clue.text: Free time with Boris and former lover – ultimately feeble erection

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so just the final letter of the word is kept
erecting raises something upright, and in a down clue raising reads the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A sniggering picture of Boris Johnson's spare time with an old flame, and a disappointing performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erection' sounds like the punchline of the joke, but in this down clue it lifts the letters upwards. Boris Johnson was UK Prime Minister 2019-22.
explanation.definitionFit: To be exempt is to be released from an obligation or rule, so not bound by it.

clue.text: Squeamishly opening arse cheek

indicators.note: an opening is the start of something, so only the first letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the American spelling of the same rude word

explanation.surface: Someone nervously parting a buttock, a typical bit of Private Eye smut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheek' sits next to 'arse' as a buttock, but it means impudence.
explanation.definitionFit: Sass is informal American slang for impudent, disrespectful back-talk, just as cheek is in Britain.

clue.text: Just lose out with sexual partner dropping one

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged
to drop something is to let it fall away, so a letter is lost

blocks.note: a means one, and this letter is the one removed

explanation.surface: Narrowly missing out as a lover walks out on you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just lose out' reads as narrowly failing, but 'Just' is the definition and 'out' rearranges the next word. A is one, the letter dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Just and solely both mean only, exclusively, nothing more than, as in 'only for you'.

clue.text: Single on date with gorgeous escort starts to get tense

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening, so only first letters are kept

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: A single person on a date with a stunning companion starts to feel nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' and 'date' sound like dating, but they are a number and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Being nervous and jumpy is to be on edge, an idiom for anxious and strained.

clue.text: Member, Conservative, involved in raising child

indicators.note: raising lifts things upward, and in a down clue that reads letters from the bottom
to be involved in something is to be inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A Tory party member helping to bring up a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' looks like a party member, a parliamentary member, but it is the slang word for penis.
explanation.definitionFit: Member is a euphemism for the penis, and the answer is the vulgar slang term for that organ.

clue.text: All at once, sadly, nude chucks one out

indicators.note: to chuck is to toss or throw about, so the letters land in another order
out means removed, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: a means one; this letter is removed

explanation.surface: A sorry scene in which a naked person throws someone out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' looks like comment on the scene, but it supplies letters. Remove A (one) from the two words and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening suddenly occurs abruptly and without warning, at a single instant.

clue.text: Leak: corrupt peers right to go

indicators.note: something corrupt is spoilt and distorted, so the letters are scrambled
what goes leaves, so this letter is removed

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right; it is removed

explanation.surface: A news leak shows crooked members of the House of Lords must be stripped of their rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peers' looks like the House of Lords, but it is just letters; drop R and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To seep is to ooze slowly through small openings, the way liquid escapes a container.

clue.text: Mark to pass round cold Pils brew?

indicators.note: brewing stirs ingredients together, so these letters get mixed up
to go round something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: to pass away is to die
C is the abbreviation for cold

explanation.surface: Mark says it's his turn to hand round a cold Pilsner lager.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a name or a sign, but it is the Gospel writer; the question mark admits he is usually counted a follower rather than one of the twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Mark the Evangelist was an early follower of Jesus, so he is an example of a Christian follower.

clue.text: Essential organs, testicles originally stored in small bottes

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter of the word is kept
something stored in a box is kept inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: little glass bottles; bottes is a misprint for bottles

explanation.surface: Body parts, especially testicles, kept in little jars, like a pathology lab.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue misspells bottles as bottes. Testicles only lend their first letter, placed inside the small bottles.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitals is an informal word for the body's vital organs, such as heart and lungs, needed for life.
